extracted.intended_audience: stakeholders in MSHA rulemaking (mine operators, industry representatives, safety professionals, petitioners, legal/compliance staff, and members of the public who submit comments)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how MSHA develops, publishes, and completes rules (NPRMs, comment periods, analyses, final rules, and emergency standards), including related public-docket practices and procedural requirements. Useful for participants preparing comments, petitions, information-collection requests, or submissions for incorporation by reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority for rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mine Act gives the Secretary of Labor authority to develop, promulgate, and revise mining health or safety standards for the protection of life and prevention of injuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking activity must be grounded in the Secretary's statutory authority under the Mine Act; rulemaking actions can include issuance of a new rule, amendment to an existing rule, or repeal of an existing rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Federal Register rulemaking documents
rubrics_metrics.description: MSHA publishes a variety of Federal Register documents including Proposed Rules, Final Rules, Technical Amendments, Petitions for Modification, Requests for Information, Advance Notices of Proposed Rulemaking, Emergency Temporary Standards, Notices and Meetings, and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These document types constitute the formal public record of agency rulemaking activity and are available (MSHA has documents published since 1994).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal rulemaking procedural steps
rubrics_metrics.description: The process includes a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), a comment period, evaluations (such as economic and risk assessment analyses), possible interim rules, and in most cases issuance of a Final Rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed descriptions and examples of different types of rules are available on Reginfo.gov FAQ and MSHA's Rulemaking FAQ page; participants should anticipate these stages and submit evidence or analysis during the comment period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency Temporary Standard (ETS) criteria and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: An ETS may be issued when the danger to miners is so grave that immediate action is necessary. An ETS can be enforced immediately while concurrently serving as a proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an ETS is issued, a final rule must be published within nine months of publication of the ETS. The authority derives from section 101(b) of the Mine Act (30 U.S.C. 811(b)) as amended by the MINER Act of 2006.

rubrics_metrics.name: Docket content and public record requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The rulemaking docket is the file in which MSHA places all of the rulemaking documents it issues (e.g., the NPRM, hearing notices, extensions of comment periods, and final rules), supporting documents that it prepares (e.g., risk assessment and economic analyses), studies that were relied on that are not readily available to the public, and all public comments related to the rulemaking (including comments received in anticipation of the rulemaking and during the comment period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Docket Management System (via regulations.gov) provides public access to the complete record of rulemakings, guidance documents, adjudicatory actions, peer reviews, data quality and other related documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference validity requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporation by reference allows agencies to meet the requirement to publish regulations by referring to materials published elsewhere; for an incorporation to be valid, the Director of the Federal Register must approve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legally, incorporated material is treated as if published in full in the Federal Register (5 U.S.C. 552(a)) and therefore has the force of law; see 1 CFR Part 51 for more information. MSHA lists standards it incorporates on Standards.gov and the CFR website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information collection requirements under the Paperwork Reduction Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency information collections must minimize duplication and burden on the public, have practical utility, and support the proper performance of the agency's mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MSHA’s Information Collection Requests (ICRs) are reviewed by OIRA and available via an ICR Dashboard; MSHA’s existing information collections are renewed every three years and must meet PRA standards when submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting analyses and materials for rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemakings are supported by supplemental materials such as regulatory economic analyses, three-year information collection renewals, quantitative risk assessments, peer review agendas, and incorporations by reference lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These supporting documents inform the agency's proposed and final rules and are typically placed in the docket so commenters and reviewers can examine the analyses underlying MSHA's regulatory choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Agenda publication practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Twice a year, each federal agency publishes a Regulatory Agenda listing all regulations that the agency plans to issue or has recently completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MSHA’s current and historical Regulatory Agendas are available (MSHA’s current agenda is found under the Department of Labor); the Agenda signals forthcoming rulemaking activity and priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public access to Federal Register materials and preambles
rubrics_metrics.description: MSHA provides access to Federal Register documents and Final Preambles and Rule Language starting in 1995.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders can review preambles and the precise regulatory text to understand agency rationale, regulatory language, and changes between proposed and final rules.
